meta.description: Not Wilde — he died in 1900. The earliest known version is Percy Colson's, in The Sketch, 13 April 1949; Reader's Digest pinned it on Wilde in 1954.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Always forgive your enemies; nothing annoys them so much'?
meta.ogDescription: Wilde died in 1900. The line first appears in 1949, from author Percy Colson — and got Wilde's name only in a 1954 Reader's Digest filler.

answer.label: Not Oscar Wilde — most likely Percy Colson
answer.sourceLine: Wilde died in 1900, and no work of his contains this line. The earliest documented version is a precept by the British author Percy Colson, printed in The Sketch of London on 13 April 1949 — and even that reads “Nothing annoys them so intensely.” The polished wording everyone quotes appears in Reader’s Digest in June 1954, where it was credited to Wilde with no citation. Quote Investigator ↗ calls Colson the leading candidate rather than a proven author, and so do we.
answer.confidenceText: No Wilde source exists; the earliest known text is Colson’s, 1949.

source.excerpt: Always forgive your enemies. Nothing annoys them so intensely.
trail: November 1911 — a precursor, different verb. Felix Grendon’s “The Cool Philosopher,” in The International (New York), vol. 3, no. 6, carries “I always forgive my enemies; nothing enrages them more.” Quote Investigator treats this as a precursor ↗, not the origin — and note it is already eleven years after Wilde’s death.

13 April 1949 — the first close match. The Sketch of London prints Percy Colson’s precept, “Always forgive your enemies. Nothing annoys them so intensely.” QI concludes: “Percy Colson is currently the leading candidate for creator” ↗.

May–June 1954 — the name swap. Reader’s Digest (vol. 64, no. 386, p. 134) runs the modern wording over Oscar Wilde’s name with no citation, and Walter Winchell’s column of 27 May 1954 broadcasts it. Both are documented by QI ↗. No evidence has ever been produced for the Wilde credit.

Today — filed under Misattributed. Wikiquote lists the line in its “Misattributed” section ↗, noting Wilde died in 1900, that QI found no significant evidence for him, that the earliest match is Colson’s 1949 precept, and that Snopes rated the attribution incorrect.
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest documented form of the saying, as quoted by Quote Investigator ↗ from The Sketch of 13 April 1949. Compare it with the famous version: the verb is intensified differently, the comma is a full stop, and there is no Oscar Wilde anywhere near it. The wording the internet quotes is first documented five years later, in 1954 — in Walter Winchell’s 27 May column, which credits it to the June Reader’s Digest filler that carries the Wilde name.

source.rightsNote: Do not assume this line is public domain. The instinct is to reason “Wilde, died 1900, therefore free” — but Wilde did not write it, so his death date is irrelevant to its status. The exact famous wording (“nothing annoys them so much”) is first documented in 1954 — in Walter Winchell’s 27 May column, which credits it to the June Reader’s Digest, whose filler item is the source of the Wilde credit — and it has no identified author, so no rights status can honestly be asserted for it. The closest documented antecedent, Percy Colson’s 1949 precept in The Sketch, was published well after 1930 and would not be public domain in the United States on age alone.

author.name: Percy Colson
author.heading: The man who probably wrote it
author.bio: Percy Colson was a British author whose books include Melba: An Unconventional Biography (1932), Victorian Portraits (1932), A Story of Christie’s (1950) and White’s, 1693–1950 (1951). In 1949 he also collaborated with the Marquess of Queensberry on Oscar Wilde and the Black Douglas — a Wilde book that, in Quote Investigator’s reading, may be the very reason his epigram drifted onto Wilde’s name. He is the leading candidate for the line, not a confirmed author: the 1949 Sketch printing is simply the earliest appearance anyone has found.

misattribution.heading: How Wilde got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a rare case where the misattribution can be dated almost to the week. The saying existed for five years under other names before a magazine filler item handed it to Oscar Wilde — and it has never been taken back.

items.why: Reader’s Digest (vol. 64, no. 386, p. 134) printed “Always forgive your enemies; nothing annoys them so much.—Oscar Wilde” with no supporting citation whatsoever. Per Quote Investigator ↗, this is where the Wilde attribution enters the record — and it is also the first appearance of the exact wording now quoted everywhere.

Days before the issue’s cover date, the columnist Walter Winchell relayed it to a mass audience: “Reader’s Digest recalls O. Wilde’s: ‘Always forgive your enemies; nothing annoys them so much.’” — his 27 May 1954 column in the Courier-Post, as documented by QI ↗. Note the word “recalls”: the line was already being treated as something Wilde was known to have said.

When The Sketch ran Colson’s precepts in April 1949, it also mentioned he was co-author of a forthcoming book titled Oscar Wilde and the Black Douglas — published that year by Hutchinson ↗. QI’s hypothesis is blunt: “Perhaps Colson’s authorship of this book about Wilde caused confusion” ↗. A name printed next to Wilde’s became a name replaced by Wilde’s.

items.who: Quotation anthologies and the modern internet
items.why: The Wilde credit was repeated in Jon Winokur’s 1987 compilation The Portable Curmudgeon and in newspapers from 1955 onward, per QI’s citation trail ↗. Wikiquote ↗, which files the line under “Misattributed,” records that an image of Wilde captioned with the quote spread online in 2022 and that Snopes rated the attribution incorrect.

misattribution.truthLine: Wilde died on 30 November 1900. The saying is not documented until April 1949, and its famous wording not until June 1954 — so whoever polished it, it was not him. Quote Investigator ↗ names Percy Colson the leading candidate, and stops there. So do we.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Wilde
lead: The epigram is built exactly the way Wilde built his: a piece of conventional moral advice, followed by a comma and a motive that ruins it. Forgiveness recast as a weapon is a very Wildean move, and that structural fingerprint is most of why the line has survived seventy years of being pinned on the wrong man. It sounds like him, so nobody checks.

But sounding like Wilde is precisely what makes an epigram dangerous to attribute. Wilde is one of the most quoted writers in English and one of the most over-quoted — a magnet name that unsourced cleverness drifts toward. The trail here is unusually well documented: a 1911 precursor using “enrages,” a 1949 precept by Percy Colson using “intensely,” and then a 1954 magazine filler that smoothed the wording to “so much” and handed the credit to a man who had been dead since 1900.
context.detailsSummary: The wording changed twice on its way to fame
detailsBody: 1911 — “enrages”: Felix Grendon’s “The Cool Philosopher,” in The International (New York, November 1911), has “I always forgive my enemies; nothing enrages them more.” First person, and a different verb. Quote Investigator treats this as a precursor, not the source.
1949 — “intensely”: Percy Colson’s precept in The Sketch reads “Always forgive your enemies. Nothing annoys them so intensely.” Second person now, and a full stop rather than a semicolon.

1954 — “so much”: Reader’s Digest prints the version we all know — semicolon, “so much” — and attributes it to Oscar Wilde. Nobody has identified who did the smoothing, which is why the exact famous wording has no known author at all.
context.pull: It sounds like Wilde. That is the whole reason it stuck — and the whole reason to check.
